name: David Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group that isn't tied to AI companies, employers or government. Nothing you say will carry your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings I'm at the desk in a unit on the industrial estate, four of us, designing shop signs, van lettering and window graphics. Afternoons, two or three days a week, I go out with Ray, the owner, to fit them: peeling vinyl, squeegeeing out bubbles on a van door in the wind. I'm still learning both sides, and Ray's patient, mostly.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what grinds you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like seeing a van I lettered drive past my dad's corner shop. What grinds me down is the pay and the hours. I rent with my cousin Bilal, I send a bit home to my mum every month, and I've got about ten days of money saved. There's one other sign firm nearby, and they're family-run, so they're not hiring outsiders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. I use it now and then to show a customer what their van will look like, and that's useful, but it was never going to fit a sign. I'd say that to Ray in the van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my job's as steady as it was, which is fine but tight. My worry is money, not robots. Sending money home and paying rent leaves me with almost nothing at the end of the month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and ask Ray if I can do more fitting days, because that's where I'm getting good. I'd try to put twenty a week aside. I'd keep using the mockup tool when a customer needs convincing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. A bit stretched, but steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You send money home. What happens if a month goes wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If one month goes wrong, it's my mum's money that gets short first, and I'd rather go hungry than let that happen. My dad would say don't worry, but I'd worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does any of the small automation touch your day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The quotes and the mockups, maybe. Ray spends evenings on quotes, so a tool that does them would help him more than me. My desk work might shrink a bit, but the fitting doesn't.

say: I'd say AI was **never going to fit** a sign.
I'd mention the **mockup tool** helps customers picture their van.
think: **Rent and money home** leave almost nothing each month.
Small tools might trim my **desk work**, not the fitting.
do: Keep using the **mockup tool** to win customers.
S0.quote: If one month goes wrong, it's my mum's money that gets short first, and I'd rather go hungry than let that happen.
fieldNote: His sense of **duty to family** shapes every money decision.
He sees **fitting work** as his safe, growing half.
He uses AI **only when it helps** close a sale.

steps.text: Ask Ray (his boss) for more van-fitting days each week
Put twenty a week into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like when the vinyl cutters came in, people adapted. Work hard, learn the useful bits, carry on. I wouldn't want the government stepping in, firms should sort it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the design half of my job shrinks. Customers will make their own sign designs on their phones and just want someone to fit them. If the shop owner designs the sign on a phone, my boss still needs someone to climb the ladder and stick it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Ray to move me onto fitting most days, and I'd learn from the AI tools once he's seen them work. I'd do a short course in vehicle wrapping, which is the harder, better-paid fitting. I'd cut my own spending, not the money home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a bit. But I've got my hands, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the design half shrinks. Does that mean less pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe at first, because I'm a learner fitter, not a skilled one. Ray pays fitters more once they're good, so it's a year or two of tight money. I'd manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Takeaways, the gym, nights out with the lads. I'd still go to Friday prayers and my mum's for Sunday dinner, that costs nothing anyway.

feel: A bit **anxious**, but glad I've **got my hands**.

fieldNote: He trusts **hands-on fitting** more than design.
He'd **protect the money home** before his own spending.
He'd adopt tools **after his boss**, not before.
He accepts a **pay dip** while he grows into skilled fitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and people need to stick together, families especially. I'd not trust the government to fix it. I'd say that to my dad and the people at the mosque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, my design work is gone in 2028. The fitting is hands-on, so I'd have until about 2031. That's three years to save and work out what's next, and three years isn't long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to fitting full time straight away, even if Ray pays less. I'd move back in with my parents to save the rent, and give my share to the house instead. I'd start working weekends at my dad's shop, learning the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not lost. I'd have work for a while, and family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: After 2031, when robots fit signs, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When robots can fit signs, I'd hope my dad's corner shop could feed us, because family is the only plan I'd trust. I'd hope the shop could feed us, but I don't really know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take any help from the government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if there was nothing else. My dad would rather we all eat less than take handouts. But if it's everyone, it's different, I suppose.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and families must **stick together**.
I'd say I **don't trust** the government to fix it.
think: Fitting gives me until about **2031**, which isn't long.
Three years is my window to **save** and plan.

**Move back** in with my parents to save rent.
feel: **Worried**, but **not lost**, with work and family for now.
S2.quote: When robots can fit signs, I'd hope my dad's corner shop could feed us, because family is the only plan I'd trust.
fieldNote: The **three-year robot gap** gives him time to save.
He resists state help, but **softens** if everyone's affected.
He'd **move home** and pay into the family house instead of rent.

steps.text: Switch to sign fitting full time, even at lower pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, so get ready. Learn something solid, save, look after your family. I'd say it at work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years means I'd be a skilled fitter by 2031. That's good money until the robots, and a few years of decent savings. Then I'd have a decision to make about my dad's shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to be the main fitter within two years. I'd do the wrapping course next year. I'd keep using the AI mockups once Ray uses them too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can see myself coping. Five years is enough to get good at something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What decision about your dad's shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether to take it on. My dad's back is bad and he wants to stop in a few years, so his corner shop might become my job anyway. I'd need to be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably get married a bit later, until I'm sure I can provide. That matters to me.

I'd tell people to **learn something solid**, save and look after family.

A few years of **decent savings** come before the robots.
do: Push to be **main fitter** within two years.
S3.quote: My dad's back is bad and he wants to stop in a few years, so his corner shop might become my job anyway.
fieldNote: Five years lets him build **real skill** and savings.

steps.text: Ask Ray to make him the main fitter within two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for anyone willing to work. Learn a trade, save, and don't wait for someone to rescue you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's comfortable enough. I'd be fitting and wrapping for years, and robots don't come for that until 2039. By then I'd be 40 and could have the shop or my own wrap business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with Ray and get good at wrapping. I'd save for a house deposit over five or six years. I'd use the AI tools as they become normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the far end, but I'm fine for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the far end you're uneasy about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2039 a robot might wrap a van better than me, and I've no idea what I'd do then. That's twelve years away, though, and I'll have the shop or the wraps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, if not yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bilal, my cousin, who's in a call centre. That's thinking work all day, so it goes in 2036. I'd tell him to learn a trade now.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because I'd only have three years of fitting and no savings. What would help is a proper apprenticeship scheme with a wage, and firms like Ray's getting help to keep training people. Family would do the rest.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the money I send home. Half the designers I know send money to their parents, so when our jobs go, it's not just us who feel it.

headlineQuote: Half the designers I know send money to their parents, so when our jobs go, it's not just us who feel it.
portrait: David is a **27-year-old junior** designer who also fits signs and van lettering.
He uses AI **now and then**, mainly for mockups to win customers.
He sends money **home to his mum** and has about ten days saved.
He values **family and self-reliance**, and distrusts government help.
His **hands-on fitting** keeps him calmer than most designers, even with fast AGI.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with only three years of fitting and no savings.
whatWouldHelp: A paid **apprenticeship scheme** and help for firms to keep training.
